articles.title: Trump promised to lower prices for Americans. Here's what the data shows.
articles.summary: Just weeks before the midterm elections, 90% of Americans say prices in the U.S. are the main factor shaping their view of the economy. These charts show why...
articles.body:
President Trump campaigned in 2024 on promises to lower Americans' cost of living, vowing to push gasoline prices below $2 a gallon and to deliver 2% mortgage rates. Two years later, consumers face sharply higher costs for many of the necessities he pledged to make more affordable.

Less than a month before the midterm elections , the gap between Mr. Trump's promises and the financial realities facing many Americans is fueling voter frustration over the economy. Although economic growth is solid and unemployment remains low, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a recent CBS News poll .

The financial pressures affecting Americans predate Mr. Trump's return to the White House last year. Consumers are reeling from the cumulative impact of five years of post-pandemic inflation, economists note. But his campaign promises raised hopes that he would lower consumer prices.

At the same time, some of Mr. Trump's policies have exacerbated inflation. His tariff regime contributed about 2.9 percentage points to inflation through February, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Without the tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.

Mr. Trump's decision to attack Iran in February has also led to a drawn-out conflict that has disrupted oil shipments and sharply driven up the price of oil, gas and diesel.

"It's undeniable that several of these supply shocks that the U.S. economy has been navigating through come from policy decisions made by the administration — namely, decisions to intervene in Iran and decisions to impose tariffs," Greg Daco, chief economist at investment advisory firm EY-Parthenon, told CBS News.

Inflation in September is forecast to have risen at an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.4% in August, according to economists polled by FactSet — well above the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.

Ryan Bourne, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, said that consumers "judge the prices they're paying against the prices they paid four or five years ago, and are still shocked by it."

He added, "As a result of that, they think the economy's doing very, very badly."

The White House said that Mr. Trump's agenda "stopped Biden's inflation crisis" while creating jobs and economic growth. The administration's policies "will continue to deliver economic wins over the next two years," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News.

"The President has delivered tangible wins for American families: He signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals that put American workers first and sent 401(k)s to record highs," Rogers added.

The following charts show how U.S. costs have changed for expenses ranging from groceries to car insurance.

"A vote for Trump means your groceries will be cheaper." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Pittsburgh on Nov. 4, 2024.

For consumers, each visit to the supermarket is a fresh reminder of inflation's impact on food costs, which have continued to rise since Mr. Trump vowed to lower grocery prices.

The cost of food prepared at home has climbed 4% since November 2024, according to Consumer Price Index data, when Mr. Trump said a vote for him would lead to lower costs. That increase comes on top of a 23% jump in food prices during the prior four years. Because consumers tend to remember what they spent on groceries before the pandemic, they get a jolt each time they visit the supermarket, said Daco of EY-Parthenon.

"Whether it's talking about gas prices or grocery prices or restaurant prices or travel prices, everybody talks about inflation," he said. "The salience of prices is what is driving this downbeat consumer morale."

Food costs are continuing to rise due to a number of factors, ranging from the elevated price of gas and diesel, which are needed to fuel farm equipment and ship items to stores, to the Trump administration's tariffs, economists said.

"Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon, bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares, and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the Economic Club of New York on Sept. 5, 2024.

Gas prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. As of Oct. 9, the national average price for a gallon of gasoline was $4.37. That's up 47% from $2.98 on Feb. 27, one day before the war began, according to CBS News data. Prices at the pump are at a record high for October, according to AAA .

Diesel prices rose to a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22 and now hover around $6.28. Diesel, which is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, is a factor in consumer prices for nearly every type of good, including groceries.

Gas prices tend to have an outsized impact on consumer sentiment, influencing their views on future inflation and the broader economy, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.

"By contrast, I'm announcing today that under my leadership, the United States will commit to the ambitious goal of slashing energy and electricity prices by half, at least half." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.

Consumers' energy bills have continued to increase this year. Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that average monthly residential electricity costs rose 12.5% between December 2024 and July of this year. Electricity bills are rising as utilities spend more to upgrade the nation's aging power grid, and overall energy demand grows amid the data center buildout.

Natural gas is also more expensive. Average monthly residential prices for natural gas rose 106% between December 2024 and July 2025, according to the EIA. Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan policy and research firm, attributes the jump to geopolitical conflict, an increase in domestic exports, extreme weather linked to climate change and rising infrastructure costs.

A July report from advocacy groups The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers found that the national average utility bill reached $280 per month in early 2026, up 12% since the end of 2024, just before Mr. Trump took office.

Many people could face even higher energy prices this winter. Americans are forecast to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes between mid-November and mid-March 2027, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, a policy organization. Homeowners who use heating oil are projected to pay an average of $2,627 over that three-month period, up roughly 50% from last year, the group said.

"Car insurance is up 70% to 100%, and you can't get it. … But prices will come down. You just watch, they'll come down, and they'll come down fast." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.

Car insurance costs are one area where consumers are seeing some modest relief. Data shows motorists are paying 5.5% less for vehicle coverage since premiums hit a recent high in February.

Still, insurance prices have soared in recent years along with the cost of both new and used vehicles. Yelena Shulyatyeva, senior U.S. economist for The Conference Board, a nonprofit that represents businesses, attributed the recent dip in premiums to increased industry competition, rather than public policy actions.

"Some of the deceleration was a result of a pushback from consumers, rather than some legislative or other action," Shulyatyeva told CBS News.

"We will drive down the rates so you will be able to pay 2% again, and we will be able to finance or refinance your homes drastically at much lower costs." — Mr. Trump at a campaign rally in Tucson, Arizona, on Sept. 12, 2024.

Mortgage rates were climbing from pandemic-era lows for several years before President Trump returned to office in January of 2025. The average rate on a conventional 30-year mortgage now stands at 7.28%, up from 7.04% when Mr. Trump took office, according to Freddie Mac.

But home loan rates have been volatile, briefly dipping below 5% in February before climbing amid surging government bond yields , rising inflation and geopolitical tensions.

Borrowing costs are just one side of the struggle: Home buyers are also contending with high prices, keeping many on the sidelines as they wait for more affordable options. The median list price for a home in August was $408,333, up 4% from $392,967 since Mr. Trump took office, according to Zillow.

The gap between the income needed to afford a home, $126,487, and the U.S. median income, $86,490, is now the widest since 2005, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

"We're going to put a temporary cap on credit card interest rates. We're going to cap it around 10%. We can't let them make 25% and 30%." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Uniondale, New York, on Sept. 18, 2024.

President Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates at 10% while campaigning, an issue he also highlighted after taking office in 2025 . But while the effort drew bipartisan support, the proposal fizzled.

Currently, the average credit card rate across all commercial bank accounts is 20.94%, down from 21.58% when Mr. Trump resumed office, according to Federal Reserve data . Credit experts said the rate-cap proposal would have hindered consumers' access to credit.

"Obviously, we'd love for everyone to have low rates and be free from debt. But the unintended consequence of a 10% cap would be the loss of access to credit, because banks say they wouldn't be profitable with it capped at that low rate," Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling firm, told CBS News.

"We're going [to] … bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the New York Economic Club on Sept. 5, 2024.

Along with promising to reduce energy prices, Mr. Trump pledged to lower airfare costs for travelers. In recent months, fares have eased slightly, although CPI data shows that they remain 17% higher than in January 2025.

The war in Iran has disrupted global oil supplies and raised jet fuel costs, which are the second- biggest expense for airlines after labor costs. Facing significantly larger fuel bills, carriers are raising prices to cover the added costs.

Jet fuel now costs $4.34 a gallon, up 85% from an average of $2.35 per gallon in January 2025, according to the Energy Information Administration. Aviation analysts also point to the May shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines as another factor behind higher fares.

"I will make the ACA much, much, much better for far less money (or cost) to our greatest American citizens. …" — Mr. Trump in a Truth Social post on March 26, 2024.

Millions of Americans with an Affordable Care Act health insurance plan face sharply higher costs than a year ago. Average monthly premiums have risen to $178, or $2,136 per year, up 58% from 2025, according to a May analysis from nonprofit health group KFF.

Obamacare plan deductibles have soared from an average of $1,027 per person to $3,786, up 37% over the same period, KFF found. Prices for ACA plans spiked after Congress allowed a tax subsidy designed to lower plan costs to expire at the end of last year.

In an effort to offer relief, the Trump administration began sending $500 checks in September to nearly 1 million ACA participants in 30 states.

"When reelected as president, I will continue my efforts to protect Americans from unaffordable drug prices …" — Mr. Trump in an interview with AARP Magazine on Oct. 2, 2024.

Prescription drug prices have dropped since Mr. Trump took office in his second term, falling 3.9% after peaking in February 2025, government data show.

Mr. Trump has credited his policies lowering drug costs, with the White House stating in August that the president "has delivered" on his campaign promise. The administration cited policies such as its "most favored nation" approach, which links U.S. drug prices to those paid in other developed nations.

Experts said that while the Trump administration's policies have helped, other factors are also at play. For instance, manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are cutting their prices amid increased competition, while the nonpartisan Brookings Institution notes that more generic drugs are entering the marketplace, tempering healthcare costs.

articles.title: GOP lawmaker urges Johnson to scrutinize new socialist lawmakers' 'access to intelligence'
articles.summary: Nicole Malliotakis warns two Democratic Socialists of America members heading to the House of Representatives pose a "national security threat."
articles.body: New York City's lone Republican in the House of Representatives is raising alarms about the far-left Democrats poised to serve alongside her on Capitol Hill next year. "These people are extreme, they're radical, they are dangerous, and they really have no business being in the United States House of Representatives," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "And it scares me that they're going to have access to intelligence." New York City was one of the largest fronts in the nationwide civil war that's gripped the Democratic Party this midterm election cycle. It's where two members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) scored upset primary victories against establishment-backed candidates — in deep-blue seats that mean they are virtually guaranteed to win their general elections in November. DEMOCRATIC CONGRESSMAN WARNS OF 'DANGEROUS' SOCIALIST AGENDA AFTER FAR-LEFT PRIMARY WINS Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chairman Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y., in his Upper Manhattan and Bronx-area district, while New York State Assemblywoman Claire Valdez won an open race for the Brooklyn- and Queens-area district represented by retiring Rep. Nydia Velazquez, D-N.Y. Both Chevalier and Valdez have called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and have called Israel's war on Gaza a "genocide." DSA CO-CHAIR MOCKED FOR PROUDLY CONFIRMING SOCIALISTS WANT TO ABOLISH THE SENATE, NATIONAL BORDERS, PRISONS Malliotakis said their support of the DSA platform made both "un-American." "I think they want to undermine the country. I mean, anybody whose campaign is based on no jails, no cops, no borders, is a real detriment to the country," she said. "These are the people that are going to have access to intelligence? I think [Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.] really needs to look at that and see if they're a national security threat." JOHNSON WARNS COMMUNISM IS 'ON OUR OWN SHORES' AFTER FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES WIN NEW YORK PRIMARIES And if Republicans win the House majority in November, she called on Johnson to limit which committees the pair could serve on. "I do have a lot of concern about these members having access to sensitive information and intelligence that if put in the wrong hands, could be a detriment to our national security," Malliotakis said. DEMOCRATIC INFIGHTING GROWS AS CONGRESSWOMAN EXPOSES ‘DISRESPECTFUL’ WELCOME OF SOCIALISTS INTO ‘BIG TENT’ The sentiment is just a preview of what is likely to be historic division within the House of Representatives next year, no matter who wins the midterms. The DSA has advocated for scrapping the U.S. Constitution in favor of a new system, as well as the abolition of prisons, the Supreme Court and the police. Malliotakis also pointed out that Chevalier once posted online, "I forgot to get napkins, so I just wiped my hand on the American flag behind me." But next year they are poised to be in the same congressional delegation, and the New York Republican, born to a Greek immigrant father and a Cuban immigrant mother, said she does not know how she could work with them. "They are so extreme, I don't see where we would find common ground," Malliotakis said. "I don't think I could work with somebody who wipes her hands on the American flag because she doesn't have a napkin." articles.title: Why it took a lawsuit to get a real investigation into Cornell
articles.summary: The decision about whether to prosecute an alleged gang rape depended on an investigation conducted by the university’s own police department. Think about that.
articles.body:
Every institution I have sued over sexual abuse says some version of the same thing when the lawsuit lands: We take this extremely seriously.

Then I get the file. And too often, what I find looks nothing like the statement the public receives.

There is often a prior complaint, a documented warning, conduct someone had already flagged, and an investigation that checked every procedural box without asking the hard questions. The decisions often make more sense as protecting the institution than protecting the person who came forward.

That is why the case unfolding at Cornell University should make people uncomfortable.

In 2024, a Cornell student went to campus police about a night at the Chi Phi fraternity house involving seven of its members . The district attorney declined to bring charges. His reason: Her sworn written statement to campus police did not allege that she had been drugged or did not consent to the sexual activity that took place.

But he has also acknowledged that his office never received the transcript of her interview with campus police before making that decision, and that prosecutors did not independently investigate. The decision not to bring charges was based on the investigation conducted by Cornell Police and the record provided to his office.

So the decision about whether to prosecute an alleged gang rape depended on an investigation conducted by the university’s own police department. Ithaca police say the case was never reported to them .

I’m not saying anyone at Cornell set out to bury the incident. I am saying no institution should be the only one holding the file on its own crisis. And for nearly two years, that was where the matter stood.

Then the student sued. Within days, the district attorney reopened the criminal investigation and said he would take the case to a grand jury. Cornell agreed to an independent review after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) called for outside scrutiny. Days later, Hochul went further, appointing Attorney General Letitia James (D) as special prosecutor in the case .

The accused deserve due process. It is up to a grand jury and the courts to decide what can be proven. But the timeline raises a harder question: Why did it take a lawsuit for everyone to look again?

Cornell isn’t unique. Universities, hospitals, churches and companies all have something to lose when serious allegations surface: reputation, trust, donors, patients, applicants or shareholders. And sometimes getting to the truth means confronting whether someone inside missed a warning, ignored a complaint or failed to act.

No one has to plot a cover-up for self-preservation to shape what happens next. A complaint gets processed. Lawyers get involved. Someone is disciplined, transferred or removed. A statement says the matter was taken seriously. The file is closed, and the institution moves on.

But the person who was harmed doesn’t get to move on. Some of the people I represent can’t walk into a doctor’s office anymore, sit in a classroom or trust anyone in authority. That doesn’t close when the file does.

A survivor who comes forward doesn’t get to hand their case to the system and go home to heal. They retell the worst night of their life to police, administrators and investigators. Then they wait for a decision. And when the file comes back closed, they’re expected to accept it.

If they don’t, they have to find a lawyer, file a lawsuit and tell the story all over again. This time, it is in public, while strangers question their motives, their memory and whether it happened at all. Sooner or later, someone calls it a cash grab.

I have represented survivors. I know what that accusation ignores: Therapy, medical care, lost work, an education or career derailed. The harm can follow people for the rest of their lives. A settlement isn’t a payday when you’re the one left paying for harm someone else caused.

These lawsuits aren’t just about money. They’re about accountability .

I have been a trial lawyer long enough to know what happens next. The institution says it investigated. I ask for the investigation. It says it followed policy. I ask for the policy and the evidence that anyone followed it. It says nobody could have known. I ask who complained before and what they did about it.

Then I ask for the emails. The texts. The disciplinary records. The internal communications. I put decision-makers under oath and ask the questions that may never have been asked before.

That’s what filing a lawsuit does. It turns “We took this extremely seriously” from a statement into something an institution has to prove.

That’s why these cases matter beyond any settlement or dollar amount. An institution can hire lawyers, issue carefully worded statements and insist it followed procedure. But if the same failures continue behind closed doors, what has actually changed?

If an institution can protect its reputation, close the file and move on without confronting what went wrong, what stops it from doing the same thing the next time? That’s how institutional failures become patterns. Not because someone necessarily ordered a cover-up, but because protecting the institution can become easier than exposing what went wrong inside it.

The institutions and allegations may change, but the fundamental problem doesn’t: The people with the most to lose from what an investigation uncovers can also be the ones conducting it.

Cornell shows where that can lead. When a university’s own police investigate allegations that could expose failures within that university, their work becomes part of what prosecutors rely on to decide what happens next. What gets documented matters. What gets handed over matters. And what never reaches the people making those decisions matters too.

Survivors are owed more than a statement saying they were taken seriously. They’re owed more than “trust us.” They’re owed a process where the institution with something to lose isn’t the one controlling what comes to light.

Elliott Jung is a partner at HHJ Trial Attorneys in San Diego, where he represents plaintiffs in personal injury cases, including survivors of sexual assault and institutional abuse.

articles.title: Stephen A. Smith says Trump’s financial pledges aren’t winning over Americans at NewsNation town hall
articles.summary: Independent political commentator Stephen A. Smith slammed President Trump over his messaging on affordability — a top issue for voters heading into the midterm elections — during a Tuesday event hosted by NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner. “Every time you see Trump, he seems to be talking to some business network or the CEOs instead…
articles.body:
Independent political commentator Stephen A. Smith slammed President Trump over his messaging on affordability — a top issue for voters heading into the midterm elections — during a Tuesday event hosted by NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner.

“Every time you see Trump, he seems to be talking to some business network or the CEOs instead of people at the kitchen table,” Smith told the outlet’s Chris Cuomo.

“That’s not how he got reelected in 2024,” the political commentator continued. “He got reelected in 2024 not just because he was able to point to the lack of attention that the Democrats were paying to issues like affordability.”

Trump largely ran on promises to bring down the cost of living during his 2024 presidential campaign, saying he would bring the price of gasoline below $2 per gallon and mortgage rates down to 2 percent.

However, the president’s approval ratings on his overall job performance and on his handling of the economy have taken a hit as costs rise amid the Iran war and his trade fight with Canada.

The president has repeatedly urged Americans to cast their votes this November as if he were “on the ballot,” even as some Republicans in battleground states seek to distance themselves from Trump’s political brand.

During the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas in September, Trump promised to pay out $5,000 checks to every U.S. adult if the Republican Party maintained control of both chambers of Congress this fall.

The president also announced earlier this month that his administration would send $90 checks to 20 million seniors enrolled in Medicare to offset premium costs.

Smith said this type of messaging is “not washing with the American people.”

“They’re not falling for that,” he continued. “They expected him to be better, and he has not given the impression that he is better.”

articles.title: Mike Pence group urges Trump to reverse Russia diesel plan
articles.summary: Advancing American Freedom, a conservative think tank founded by former Vice President Pence, is calling on the Trump administration not to allow Russia to ship unsanctioned diesel to the U.S., according to a letter obtained by The Hill. The GOP group joins some Senate Republicans and others who have pushed back on the diesel deal. …
articles.body:
Advancing American Freedom, a conservative think tank founded by former Vice President Pence, is calling on the Trump administration not to allow Russia to ship unsanctioned diesel to the U.S., according to a letter obtained by The Hill. The GOP group joins some Senate Republicans and others who have pushed back on the diesel deal.

“The way to cheaper diesel is more American drilling and refining,” the authors wrote. “Paying [Russian President Vladimir] Putin blood money for fuel America already exports is wrong, illegal and stupid.”

The authors, including Richard Stern, argue that importing Russian oil would not actually help global oil markets but instead would give Russia the economic backing for its war with Ukraine. They also lay out how laws passed by Congress bar Russia from selling any diesel to the U.S.

Trump announced last week that Russia would ship diesel to the U.S., and the administration suspended sanctions on that diesel through next year, in an effort to bring down high diesel and fuel costs in the U.S. The economic effects of those prices are threatening Republicans’ midterm odds.

But the solution, many Republicans say, is not turning to Putin.

Trump’s occasional openness to negotiating with Putin has come under fire from some Republicans in his coalition, especially those who are strong backers of Ukraine. When Trump signaled interest last month in inviting Putin to the Group of 20 summit in Miami, several Senate Republicans joined Democrats in criticizing the move.

articles.title: Judge extends White House access for US media outlets amid Trump standoff
articles.summary: CNN, MS Now and Politico can continue to access White House as judge maintains Trump’s ban likely illegal.
articles.body:
A federal judge has extended access to several media organisations that United States President Donald Trump had sought to ban from the White House.

US District Judge Timothy Kelly said Trump likely broke the law in banning journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico from attending White House briefings.

The decision, published late Tuesday, expands on an emergency order issued by Kelly on September 24 that temporarily reinstated access to organisations. It said Trump likely discriminated against the news organisations based on their viewpoints, in violation of the First Amendment of the US Constitution.

He wrote that Trump’s “announcement of the ban and later remarks explaining the reason for it make this a straightforward conclusion: President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him”.

In announcing the ban, Trump had said the organisations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States”.

The Department of Justice subsequently said the reporters’ White House passes were revoked on national security grounds.

In his ruling, Kelly rejected the claim.

“First, there is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision,” he wrote.

The latest order stands until Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during the president’s first term, makes a final determination in the case, or until an appeals court steps in.

Trump has long been a critic of legacy US media and has previously sought to restrict access to certain organisations.

He has also lodged rhetorical attacks on individual reporters both in person and on social media, while launching an array of lawsuits against media companies.

Speaking during an October 8 hearing, Theodore Boutrous, a lawyer for the three banned organisations, said Trump was seeking to “coerce better coverage”.

The Freedom of the Press Foundation was among the groups cheering the latest court ruling.

“But this fight is far from over,” senior adviser for advocacy Caitlin Vogus said in a statement.

“We have every reason to expect the administration will appeal Kelly’s latest order and also continue to prevent CNN and Politico from participating in pool coverage of the president,” she said. “Trump must not be allowed to trample on fundamental First Amendment protections by handpicking his press corps or turning pool duties into a reward for favorable coverage.”

articles.body: Protesters repeatedly interrupted War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s headline appearance at the Army’s biggest annual conference on Wednesday, calling him a "war criminal" and a "coward" in protest of the Iran war. At least five times in the first half hour of a panel, foul-mouthed anti-war protesters shouted at Hegseth, calling him a "f---ing Nazi" among other insults. Hegseth responded with chuckles and sarcastic comments, at first — but his reactions became increasingly short and irritated as he slammed the "semi-coordinated" attack as one-by-one protesters emerged among the crowd in Washington, D.C. "Children in Gaza are starving! He is a war criminal!" "She thinks highly of me," the Pentagon chief quipped after one outburst, which led to brief applause from the crowd. The protesters were spread among the room and waited a few minutes between outbursts to interrupt the panel with their anti-war messages. As Hegseth saw a pattern emerging among the outbreaks, he acknowledged: "Appears we have a bit of a tactic." "The protesters are spouting off slogans, Iran really will never have a nuclear weapon," he later added. "The acting Army Secretary organized, and we were honored to host, a historic forum to discuss a critical issue that directly affects national security. We’re grateful for the swift action of security and the Metropolitan Police Department to ensure this important discussion could continue." The panel with Hegseth included acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink and assistant Secretary for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict Derrick Anderson. As the disruptions continued, the speakers stopped pausing amid the din of shouting and tried to talk over the protesters. It’s unclear how the protesters received credentials to attend the event known as AUSA, which largely brings together Army brass and the defense contractors that service them. The event set an attendance record of 41,000 people this year. The data gathered on the voters and donors included names, dates of birth, physical addresses, emails, whether the person was a registered Republican, their occupation and place of employment — samples on the list included retirees, pool technicians, drivers, loggers, etc. — credit card information, donor analysis data and donation amount, among other details. JACK SMITH'S TRUMP PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS AS INVESTIGATION WENT BEYOND LAWMAKERS Fox News Digital reached out to Smith’s newly launched law firm for comment. The memo follows a previous release from Grassley that showed Smith’s team collected checks from nearly 5,000 Americans across the country who donated to Trump and Trump-aligned Republican entities. "This update shows that Jack Smith and the Biden Justice Department collected incredibly invasive donor data — and voter data — beyond what could conceivably be necessary for him or his team to fulfill the [special counsel office’s] mandate," Grassley said. HOUSE VOTES TO REPEAL CONTROVERSIAL ARCTIC FROST PROVISION FROM GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BILL "This update further corroborates that Smith and his partisan team aimed to map out the entire Republican Party apparatus," he continued. "I again call on my Democratic colleagues to join my oversight work instead of trying to defend Smith and sweep his abuse of authority under the rug." Grassley noted that during Smith’s hearing last month, he pressed the former special counsel for a "yes or no" answer on whether his investigation gathered data on donors. articles.title: Pedro Sánchez apuesta por Margarita Robles y Félix Bolaños para su lista electoral por Madrid
articles.standfirst: La actual ministra de Defensa sería su número dos, seguida del ministro de Presidencia
articles.summary: La actual ministra de Defensa sería su número dos, seguida del ministro de Presidencia
articles.body: Es uno de los asuntos de la última semana: el adelanto electoral de Pedro Sánchez, presidente del Gobierno, al próximo domingo, 29 de noviembre. Pues bien, según recoge el Diario ABC, el jefe del Ejecutivo habría aprovechado su agenda de Gobierno para terminar de decidir quiénes representarán al PSOE de cara al 29N en algunos de los puestos más simbólicos de las candidaturas a las Cortes. Como bien apunta el citado rotativo, la intención de Sánchez es que Margarita Robles sea la número dos del actual presidente del Gobierno en las listas por Madrid. El líder del Ejecutivo vuelve a confiar en la ministra de Defensa, que ya ocupó ese puesto en las elecciones de 2016. Un total de once ministros acompañarán en total a Sánchez en las listas de la formación roja de cara al 29N. Félix Bolaños, ministro de Presidencia, repetirá de número tres, al igual que en 2023. Por otro lado, José Manuel Albares, ministro de Asuntos Exteriores, Unión Europea y Cooperación, se intercambiará con Fernando Grande-Marlaska: el ministro de Interior pasará de encabezar la lista por Cádiz a ir en la quinta plaza por Madrid. Además, entre otros nombres que figuran aparecen: Borja Cabezón, adjunto a la secretaría de Organización del PSOE; la secretaria de Organización del PSOE madrileño, Pilar Sánchez Acera; y la secretaria general de Juventudes Socialistas, Aranzazu Figueroa, que ha llamado la atención de Sánchez. Los ministros Óscar López, Ángel Víctor Torres, Diana Morant, Óscar Puente, Jrodi Hereu, entre otros, ya habían anunciado a lo largo de los últimos días que no iban a concurrir en las listas. Con esta estrategia, Sánchez pretende consolidar el liderazgo de su equipo con una candidatura que combine continuidad, pocos cambios, experiencia política y representación territorial, con el objetivo de reforzar las opciones electorales del PSOE.

articles.title: Jen Psaki mocks Trump’s new press secretary, questions if she’s a 'potentially fake lawyer'
articles.summary: Jen Psaki questioned Katie Zacharia's legal credentials on her show, prompting the new White House press secretary to defend her law background.
articles.body: Former Biden White House press secretary Jen Psaki mocked President Donald Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia on Tuesday, following Zacharia's first White House briefing. Psaki questioned Zacharia's legal credentials after citing reports that researchers could not verify her admission to a state bar. The former Biden White House press secretary also criticized Zacharia's handling of her first briefing and suggested Trump had appointed someone whose legal qualifications remained unclear. "So where exactly is Katie Zacharia licensed to practice law? It is a very weird mystery, right? ... A potentially fake lawyer? I don't know. She could answer the questions and provide clarity," Psaki said during her show, "The Briefing with Jen Psaki." HOCHUL'S OFFICE MOCKS KATIE ZACHARIA WITH AARON RODGERS INJURY POST DESPITE GOVERNOR'S PRESS SECRETARY SCANDAL Zacharia responded to the criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital, defending her professional experience. "I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Zacharia said. Zacharia earned her Juris Doctorate from Pepperdine University in 2011, the White House press office said. The university confirmed her educational background in a statement published following her appointment. Pepperdine President Jim Gash, who previously worked with Zacharia when she served as his research assistant at the university's law school, praised her following Trump's announcement. "Pepperdine is proud to count Katie among our alumni, former colleagues and friends," Gash said. "As she takes on this significant responsibility, we pray that God will grant her wisdom and courage. We look forward to seeing her use her incredible gifts and extensive experience in service to our nation." KAROLINE LEAVITT JOINS FOX NEWS AS CONTRIBUTOR AFTER LEAVING WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY ROLE Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre also defended Zacharia in a statement to Fox News Digital, criticizing Psaki's television career and her handling of the White House briefing room under former President Joe Biden. "Jen Psaki's doing what she does best — trying to circle back to relevance to save her failing show," she said. "Katie Zacharia is an unwavering supporter of President Trump and a sharp communicator; she deserves credit for jumping into the pit on her first day to face the media Psaki and Biden spent years dodging." Psaki suggested she missed Zacharia's predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, before playing clips from the new press secretary's introductory remarks. After Zacharia thanked Trump for appointing her and expressed enthusiasm about joining the administration, Psaki criticized her delivery. "Oh, Katie, Katie, Katie, I am so deeply uncomfortable already, and I've watched it multiple times today," Psaki said. "Read all those words all by yourself without having to sound anything out, at least not while standing behind the podium, maybe BEFORE." KAROLINE LEAVITT'S REPLACEMENT AS PRESS SECRETARY FACES 'CRITICAL' TEST AS MIDTERMS LOOM, TRUMP ADVISOR SAYS Following the briefing, Trump praised his new press secretary when reporters asked about her performance. "I thought she was very good," Trump said. The White House issued a statement Tuesday praising Zacharia's introductory briefing and highlighting her remarks about the administration's agenda, media access and support for working parents. "The briefing, which generated wall-to-wall coverage, served as a strong introduction to her tenure and highlighted the Trump Administration’s record of delivering historic successes for the American people."

articles.title: Dem senator's hiring announcement sparks GOP eruption over who is encouraged to apply: 'Blatantly illegal'
articles.summary: Ed Markey's internship post encouraging BIPOC and LGBTQ+ applicants sparked accusations of discrimination and claims he violated civil rights law.
articles.body: A Democratic senator is facing accusations of racial and sexual discrimination over a controversial social media post encouraging members of minority groups to apply for a role in his office. "I’m hiring motivated and eager interns for the Spring 2027 semester in my Boston office. BIPOC, LGBTQ+, working class, veterans and other underrepresented candidates with Massachusetts ties are encouraged to apply," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., posted to X on Tuesday. "Are white men allowed to apply, Senator?" Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, shot back on X Tuesday. DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH Conservatives on X erupted with anger over the post, with some going as far as to claim the senator’s job posting was illegal. "Crazy that a United States Senator can openly violate civil rights law on Twitter," conservative activist Chris Rufo wrote. "This is blatantly illegal," Katie Miller, podcaster and wife of White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, wrote. NEW YORK TIMES SUED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OVER ALLEGED 'DEI-RELATED' EMPLOYMENT DISCRIMINATION The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has stated in past guidance that encouraging applicants from certain backgrounds to apply for a job does not necessarily violate federal discrimination law. However, the agency also warns that job advertisements expressing preferences based on race, sex or other protected characteristics may be unlawful. The Congressional Accountability Act also applies federal workplace discrimination protections to congressional offices. The actual job posting on Markey’s Senate website does not bar White people from applying, despite questions raised by Gill and others about whether certain applicants were being favored. Other conservatives stopped short of accusing Markey of breaking the law, but characterized his hiring practices as unjust nonetheless. "You'll notice it's never ‘I'm resigning my Senate seat because white men have too much power’ or 'I'm donating my house to reduce the racial wealth gap,’" online commentator Bernard Stanford wrote. "That would at least be a personal decision. But no — the white male sacrificial burden is always foisted upon someone else." DEMOCRATS’ GENERATIONAL BATTLE ERUPTS AS 80-YEAR-OLD SENATOR FACES YOUNGER CHALLENGER "Democrats will write stuff like this and then wonder why young white straight men have rejected their party in droves," journalist Corey Walker said. "This is disturbing, especially from the Ranking Member of the Senate Small Business Committee," Small Business Administration Administrator Kelly Loeffler posted to her X account. "From day one we’ve said it: politicians need to stop picking winners and losers — and stop turning every government program into a DEI grift. America’s entrepreneurs compete on merit, not identity. That principle should be nonnegotiable for anyone entrusted with shaping our nation’s small business policy." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Markey’s office did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

articles.title: James Talarico torches Biden border policies in stunning attack ad as progressive tries to flip Texas blue
articles.summary: James Talarico slams Joe Biden on border security in a new ad, but a 2019 interview shows he called to slash Texas' entire $800 million budget.
articles.body: Texas Democrat candidate for U.S. Senate James Talarico appears to be further moderating his previous left-wing stances as he slammed former President Joe Biden for ‘failing us’ on border security in a new campaign advertisement released Monday. Despite spewing a seemingly hawkish and downright right-leaning border stance in the recent ad, Talarico previously called to slash Texas’ entire border-security budget in an unearthed interview. "I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border," Talarico says in the opening of the ad released this week. But Talarico’s campaign couldn’t give Fox News Digital an example of him ever publicly criticizing Biden during his presidency. And the Texas Democrat explicitly made a call to put Texas’ entire $800 million two-year border security budget toward public education in a 2019 interview with The Austin Chronicle. JAMES TALARICO ADMITS DEMOCRATS TOOK ‘BORDER FOR GRANTED’ UNDER BIDEN "We're also sending about $800 million per biennium to the border with Mexico for ‘increased border security,’" Talarico said in the more than seven-year-old interview. The two-year deal allocating $400 million per year toward border security in the state of Texas was the state’s entire budget toward warding off illegal immigration at the time Talarico made the call to replace that funding. "I'd rather take that money and put it back into public education and help increase the basic allotment, for instance," he said in the interview. Talarico has ramped up his efforts to come off more moderate amid claims that he is too progressive to win a Senate seat in notoriously red Texas. His move to a more moderate stance on immigration only started during his Senate bid in the state with the highest rates of illegal immigration. "Putting a bunch of boats, planes and border patrol agents on the physical border is expensive and also does not solve the problem," he said in the interview. His 2019 criticism of border enforcement comes to the surface as border crossings under the Trump administration fell to a new record low level in 55 years in 2025, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The decline in illegal immigration followed a series of immigration enforcement measures implemented by the administration. "Everyone will admit it's just political grandstanding," Talarico said in the interview. "Certain lawmakers want to appease extreme parts of their base. And they do it by pumping money we don't have down to the border." EXCLUSIVE: TALARICO CAUGHT ON TAPE GIGGLING ABOUT HIS CHURCH HOUSING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS SET FOR DEPORTATION In his run for Senate, Talarico has now labeled himself a "border security" Democrat, despite an extensive history of pushing back on border security reform and authorities. A former member of the Texas legislature and a former school teacher, Talarico has been in the spotlight repeatedly for many of his far-left controversies, particularly comments regarding immigration enforcement. He has called to dismantle Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), claiming it was "time to tear down this secret police force." Talarico also referred to illegal aliens as his "constituents." He labeled Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s border security policies as "atrocities" and accused him of "hunting" illegal immigrants. The Senate candidate also said he "taught a lot of undocumented students," and that those illegal aliens were more patriotic than Americans. "James is proud to be the only candidate in this race who has unveiled a border security agenda endorsed by Republican and Democratic border county sheriffs," Talarico's campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told Fox News Digital when asked about the flip-flop. TALARICO DISAPPEARANCE HAS DEM VOLUNTEERS WORRYING AND TRUMP ASKING, 'WHAT IS GOING ON?' He continued, "James supports stronger border security and immigration enforcement — it’s why he’s called for more border patrol agents and has said we should be arresting and deporting violent criminals and human traffickers — not moms and babies." The Texas Senate hopeful went briefly missing from the campaign trail this month, prompting viral rumors online to swirl that he was at a behavioral health center. Talarico debunked these claims after clearing the air on his whereabouts when he reappeared Friday, reassuring voters that he was recovering from the flu. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Talarico is running against GOP rival Ken Paxton for the Senate seat in Texas. The race has remained close as November’s midterms approach.

articles.title: ‘Paid for the bullets’: Dem challenger hits senator with stunning ICE accusation during fiery Senate debate
articles.summary: Troy Jackson accused Susan Collins of paying for the bullets that killed Johan Sebastián Guerrero, igniting a fierce clash over ICE funding.
articles.body: Fierce disagreement broke out on the debate stage on Tuesday evening as Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, defended her record against accusations that she had enabled the death of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Troy Jackson, her Democratic opponent, argued Collins had facilitated the deadly encounter on the three-month anniversary of the incident by funding what he described as a "rogue agency." "Look, Senator Collins paid for the bullets and at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger," Jackson said, referring to the roughly $70 billion in funding for immigration enforcement agencies included in the Secure America Act, a party-line bill that extended provisions for the agency through the end of Trump’s term. TRUMP TAKES ICE SHUTDOWNS OFF THE TABLE WITH SIGNATURE ON KEY $70B BILL "That's the choice on this stage. A senator who helps Donald Trump hurt Maine then tells us how concerned she is, or somebody who will stand up against him before another family in Maine has to pay the price." Guerrero’s shooting has become a flash point in Trump’s immigration enforcement push, especially in the Maine Senate race where Democrats have used his death to illustrate broader critiques of Collins: that her occasional willingness to break with the majority of the GOP hasn’t meaningfully curbed the administration’s policies. But at the debate on Tuesday evening, the third between Collins and Jackson, Collins pushed back on the narrative, arguing that her power as a Republican senator has been key to implementing a handful of safeguards on an agency that she described as critical to American safety. "After the Biddeford shooting, I called the Secretary of Homeland Security, [and] met with the acting director and suggested that they prioritize Maine for receipt of these body-worn cameras. And they did. And every ICE agent in the state of Maine and across the country now has the body-worn cameras," Collins said at the debate on Tuesday. "I increased by 17% the budget for the independent Office of Inspector General," Collins added. Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian national, was fatally shot in Biddeford on July 13 when he tried to flee ICE officers in a vehicle during an operation targeting an illegal immigrant with a final order of removal, according to the Department of Homeland Security. Guerrero was not the target of the operation. 'SQUAD' MEMBER CALLS DHS 'GREATEST THREAT TO OUR SAFETY' AFTER ICE-INVOLVED SHOOTING "The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and, fearing for public safety, an officer discharged his weapon. The driver of the vehicle was struck and emergency services were immediately contacted. He passed away from his injuries," DHS said in a statement at the time. In Jackson’s estimation, the moment is emblematic of what he described as an agency out of control. "That is why I believe that this agency is just a rogue agency that's doing Donald Trump's bidding," Jackson said. "I do believe it's important to get rid of it and take that money and prioritize it into existing law enforcement that actually people believe in." Like many progressives, Jackson has argued that the agency is beyond the scope of reform, sharing the view of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The group, which backed Jackson in his gubernatorial bid earlier this year before he became a candidate for Senate, calls the agency "a violent and illegitimate agency." Jackson has shared almost that exact framing, similarly stating that ICE "is not legitimate law enforcement," in a debate from last Thursday. Collins disagrees. On Tuesday, she argued that the agency, although flawed, serves an important role in American law enforcement, pointing out that its role overlaps with many other forms of law enforcement. "It investigates child trafficking, human trafficking and general child exploitation: drug smuggling, international cartels, financial scams. It recently helped shut down a child pornography ring in the state of Maine. I don't think any of us wants to go back to the days of completely open, uncontrolled borders. That is dangerous for us," Collins argued. EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think what happened is far too many ICE officers were hired and deployed without adequate vetting and training. But let us not forget the important work that ICE does, which is why it should be reformed and not abolished, as Troy has said." Having secured their parties’ respective nominations, Collins and Jackson will face off in the state’s Nov. 3 general election. Elaine Mallon contributed to this report.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s SpaceX imposes stunning restrictions on Ukraine that could have deadly consequences
articles.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX imposed a new speed limit on Starshield satellite service that Ukraine says is disrupting drone intercepts and military operations.
articles.body: Ukraine is urgently pressing Elon Musk’s SpaceX to reverse new restrictions on its Starshield satellite service that Kyiv warns could hamper its ability to intercept Russian attack drones and conduct other military operations, a source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital. The restrictions were imposed without advance warning despite Ukraine relying on the service under arrangements contracted through the U.S. government meant to last until May 15, 2027, according to the source. Ukrainian forces discovered the change overnight after experiencing connectivity problems and contacting SpaceX customer support. They were told Starshield service would be restricted on platforms traveling at speeds of 100 miles per hour or higher, the source said. RUSSIA MAY BE USING HIDDEN 'LUNCHBOX-SIZE' DRONE DEVICES TO COUNTER UKRAINE DEFENSES: EXPERT Hours later, Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said connectivity at speeds below the new threshold was being restored, while making clear that Kyiv was still seeking removal of the speed restriction itself. "Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored," Fedorov wrote on X Wednesday. "Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense." "Thank you, @elonmusk," Fedorov added. "We hope for your continued support." Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, warned that the change could particularly hamper Ukraine’s efforts to intercept Russia’s newer, jet-powered Shahed attack drones, saying it threatened "one of our few chances to defend the country" against them. Ukrainian forces have also begun documenting effects on the battlefield. Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Response Corps said one unmanned systems unit on the Huliaipole front had already been forced to cancel missions because of connectivity problems. The unit reported interruptions even while drones were traveling below the stated 100 mph threshold. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., pressed SpaceX for answers on X. "I'm confident this does not reflect a change in SpaceX policy because if so, intentionally degrading Ukraine's ability to defend itself might be construed as aiding and abetting a mass murderer. Can you confirm that's not SpaceX’s intent?" Starshield is SpaceX's national security satellite service, based on technology developed for the company's better-known Starlink network. The change could affect Ukrainian drones, aircraft and helicopters that rely on Starshield connectivity while moving at high speeds, including drones used to intercept Russian Shahed attacks. Ukrainian units had reported performance problems even at speeds below the stated threshold, according to the source. UKRAINE SEEKS MORE US PATRIOT INTERCEPTORS AS BOMB SHELTER PROBE DEEPENS Ukraine has contacted SpaceX seeking an explanation for the restrictions and asking the company to restore its previous service capabilities, the source familiar with the move told Fox News Digital. They said Ukraine communicated to Musk's company that the restriction had not previously applied to its terminals and was creating significant operational problems for Ukrainian forces in its continued war with aggressor Russia. Kyiv also noted that its current service arrangements, contracted through the U.S. government until May 15, 2027, cover land-based mobile and fixed uses, including mobile platforms, according to the source. SpaceX had not responded to Ukraine’s request as of Wednesday morning, the source said. PENTAGON CONSOLIDATES DRONE OVERSIGHT AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PUSHES RAPID UNMANNED WARFARE EXPANSION Polish Foreign Minister Radislaw Sikorski tore into Musk over the restrictions. "Hey @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, wea are watching you," he wrote on X. Poland pays for more than 2,900 Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine. Sikorski and Musk clashed last year over Ukraine’s dependence on Starlink, with Musk telling Sikorski, "Be quiet, small man." Fox News Digital has reached out to the Pentagon, White House and SpaceX for details. There’s been no public confirmation that Musk personally ordered the restrictions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Pentagon, through Space Force, contracts with SpaceX for Starshield services, giving the department a direct role in administering the government’s agreements with the company. But the existence of a Pentagon contract does not establish whether the military or SpaceX has authority over specific operational restrictions, including the new speed limit.

articles.title: DOJ issues subpoenas in investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar’s immigration status, including to her family members
articles.summary: The Justice Department on Friday issued about a dozen subpoenas as part of an investigation into Rep.
articles.body: The Justice Department on Friday issued about a dozen subpoenas as part of an investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, including to members of her family, a person familiar with the investigation said. The congresswoman herself was not subpoenaed, the source said, adding that the orders seeking information are tied to a federal grand jury in Minnesota, Omar’s home state. The investigation is examining matters surrounding Omar’s immigration status, and that includes, but is not limited to, her birthdate, the source said. Omar, who was born in Somalia and moved to the United States with her family in the 1990s, was naturalized when she was 17 years old, meaning she was a juvenile and able be conferred citizenship through a parent. Investigators are attempting to speak with Omar’s sister but have not issued her subpoena yet, the source said. The investigation is seeking information to see where it leads, the source said. For example, if records, representations related to age and immigration status contain false information, that would provide material for investigators to scrutinize further. They could also examine communications related to such matters. The Justice Department declined to comment to NBC News, and a spokesperson for Omar didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the subpoenas. The subpoenas came just days before federal agents searched Omar’s Washington, D.C., home as part of a yearslong criminal investigation that is partly looking into immigration fraud, a person familiar with the matter said. The investigation, which is being conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, the U.S. attorney in Minneapolis and the Justice Department, has involved whistleblowers, documents and witness testimony, the source added. After the search of her house Monday, Omar said in a statement on X, “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.” Asked Monday if he had been aware of the search in advance, President Donald Trump said the federal government was looking at Omar “very carefully.” He also repeated is frequent attacks on her and Somalia more broadly, calling her a “terrible person” who came from a nation that’s a “non-country.” “Then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution,” Trump said. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ.” That evening, Trump also attacked Omar in remarks at a rally he held for Republicans in Ohio. “I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: She’s a disaster,” Trump said. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right.’” Omar, who is part of a group of progressive women in Congress known as the “squad,” has been a frequent target of Trump’s rhetoric against her and other members’ liberal positions, as well as Somalian immigrants broadly. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appeared to tease federal action against Omar last month when he said “something’s going to happen” with her, but they were still investigating. “If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case,” Mullin said. “It’s an actual case because they did things wrong. If you decided to break the law or lie [about] the information you gave the United States to be able to come into the United States through either asylum or because you were just wanting to seek a better life, but you didn’t tell us who you actually were, you lied about certain things about your application — those things, there’s no expiration to that.”

articles.title: Vance takes aim at soft-on-crime Dems as GOP faces uphill midterm battle: ‘Lost their minds’
articles.summary: JD Vance rallied for Ken Paxton in Tyler, Texas, while taking aim at Democrats over Somali gang violence in Minnesota and spiking gas prices.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: TYLER, Texas — Faced with an uphill battle in November's midterms as costs soar for Americans, Vice President JD Vance is making a pitch that the alternative is not better and argued that Democrats would only make existing problems like street crime worse. "It sort of drives home how the Democrats have kind of lost their minds," Vance told Fox News Digital Tuesday when asked about a recent rash of Somali gang violence in Minnesota. "And if you elect Democrats, you're fundamentally electing people who will invite criminals into your state, into your communities and make your communities less safe." In typically blue Minnesota, Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is vying for a seat in the U.S. Senate but is facing a tough challenge from Republican Michele Tafoya. 100-SHOT SOMALI GANG GUN BATTLE ROCKS MINNESOTA AS SHERIFF WARNS 'WE'RE IN TROUBLE' "If you elect Republicans, you may not agree with us on everything, but we agree on some basic principles," Vance continued. "Like, for example, everybody should be safe. Everybody should be secure in their communities, and we don't want let violent criminals come into our country. "So, I do think that contrast is driven a little bit more starkly given what's happening in Minnesota." Fox News Digital spoke with the vice president after a campaign rally in the town of Tyler, Texas, about 100 miles east of Dallas, Tuesday. There, Vance rallied for Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton who is also in a tight U.S. Senate race with Democrat state Rep. James Talarico. FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON The progressive candidate recently returned from a two-week campaign absence, which Vance described as "odd." "How old is he? Thirty-five? Forty?" Vance asked about Talarico. "You've got to have the energy to do the job, and taking two weeks off the campaign in October — that's the meat of the campaign — I just think it's a very, very bizarre thing." The vice president added that he hopes Talarico's health is OK but that Texans must weigh whether he has the energy to do the job as a U.S. Senator. TALARICO DISAPPEARANCE HAS DEM VOLUNTEERS WORRYING AND TRUMP ASKING, 'WHAT IS GOING ON?' In that race, Talarico has demanded a debate with Paxton, who has yet to oblige. President Donald Trump said the two should debate, posting to Truth Social that Paxton is "ready, willing, and able." Vance took a softer stance when asked about a potential debate. "That's ultimately something Ken Paxton and James Talarico are going to decide," Vance told Fox News Digital, adding that Paxton will make a "great senator." "Obviously, those are some … things the campaigns have to negotiate," he continued. "But I'll let Ken Paxton and James Talarico make that decision. Ultimately, they each have to make their case to the people of Texas." Nationwide, Republicans are underwater when it comes to the economy and cost of living, along with the war in Iran, according to Fox News polling. REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY. Of those polled in September, 61% say gas prices are a major problem, up from 48% from two years ago, while 52% say the same for healthcare costs, up from 44%. Majorities also view housing costs (54%, down from 60%) and grocery prices (62%, down from 66%) as major problems ahead of the November election. In a similar poll, 71% of respondents said the Trump administration lacks a concrete strategy for ending the ongoing war in Iran. The two issues are closely related after gas prices spiked sharply from a national average of $2.98 per gallon at the start of the war earlier this year to an average of $4.33 per gallon today. "Well, we obviously want gas prices to be as low as they possibly can," Vance said. "And I think voters have to ask themselves, ‘Who has affirmatively taken steps to lower gas prices in the face, of course, of the Iranians terrorizing international shipping?’" REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS BREAK WITH TRUMP ON DIESEL DEAL WITH RUSSIA Vance accused Democrats of complaining about the problem without offering solutions. "We saw the president's announcement, with Russian diesel being allowed to come into the market," he said. "We have massive refinery capacity that we're announcing that we're going to build upon here. So, we're doing everything that we can, recognizing that building out energy refining capacity takes some time. "I'm very cognizant that a lot of Americans are struggling with high gas prices," he acknowledged. "We're doing as much as we can to address as much of the pain as possible." The 50th vice president stopped short of providing a definitive end date or marker that would signify an end to the war but said Iran must commit "not to rebuild [uranium enrichment] capacity and to stay off a pathway of nuclear weapons." articles.title: Hochul deflects when pressed on ties to 'anti-Christian' Mamdani in fiery debate moment: 'Shame on you'
articles.summary: New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul was pressed on her endorsement of Mayor Zohran Mamdani after Bruce Blakeman called him an antisemite.
articles.body: New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul declined to directly defend socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during Tuesday night's gubernatorial debate after her Republican challenger accused him of being antisemitic, anti-Christian and un-American. "With all the issues that face New York City, the first thing he did was sign an executive order to water down the definition of antisemitism, shame on you, mayor," Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman said on the debate stage before pointing his attention at Hochul over her endorsement of the socialist New York City mayor. "You are campaigning around the state with a guy who doesn't believe in American values," Blakeman said. "He talks about collectivism. That means you take personal property rights away. You take other people's property rights. This is a guy that's anti-Christian, couldn't find an hour out of his day to attend the installation of a new archbishop here in New York City, the biggest religion in the city of New York. Look, if you want to campaign with him, that's fine. But I will tell you right now, I think Zohran Mamdani is an antisemite. I believe he's anti-Christian. And I don't think he has American values." Hochul responded by turning to the moderator and deciding to answer a previous question about comments, reported by the New York Times, Blakeman made in a "secret meeting" related to whether the NYPD under Mamdani would respond if far-left protesters were causing violence against the Jewish community. Blakeman disputed her characterization of that meeting before complimenting Mamdani for selecting and keeping Jessica Tisch as NYPD commissioner. "Let's move on," the moderator then said. SCHUMER, JEFFRIES DODGE MAMDANI CONTROVERSY AS FELLOW NEW YORK DEM UNLOADS "Antisemitism is on the rise, and it's occurred under your watch, and Zohran Mamdani is fueling it," Blakeman added before the conversation moved to another topic. Republicans quickly highlighted the exchange on social media. HOCHUL'S OFFICE MOCKS KATIE ZACHARIA WITH AARON RODGERS INJURY POST DESPITE GOVERNOR'S PRESS SECRETARY SCANDAL "Zohran Mamdani is an antisemite, he’s anti-Christian, and he’s anti-American. And Kathy Hochul is campaigning with him," Kristin Cianci, Northeast Comms Director for the Republican National Committee (RNC) posted on X. "What an utter disgrace. New York deserves better." "Zohran Mamdani is an antisemite, anti-Christian and anti-American," the New York Republican Party posted on X. "And he's Kathy Hochul's best friend. " CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hochul was asked about the exchange and why she "didn't defend the mayor" by a reporter on Wednesday morning during a press conference on the state's investment into the first-ever community center in Jackson Heights. "I’m not going to take the bait from someone who’s throwing out such insane arguments," Hochul said. "He had a litany of things that were either false or so absurd that I’m not going to dignify them with a response from me, the governor. So, everyone knows I reject that, his description of the mayor. The mayor and I are great partners, we’re working hard together. And I’m not gonna give him the dignity of responding to those kind of crazy comments. And that’s pretty consistent how I’ve been." The two New York politicians clashed on a variety of issues on Tuesday night, including President Donald Trump, a recent ICE-involved shooting, energy prices, and inflation. Democrats outnumber Republicans by a roughly two-to-one margin in blue-leaning New York state, but polling in September indicated that Blakeman has cut his deficit against Hochul to single digits. Hochul, who is running for a second full four-year term steering the nation's fourth most populous state, stood at 50% support among likely voters in New York, with Blakeman at 41%, according to a Siena College poll conducted Sept. 11-17. By a 50%-30% margin, voters said Mamdani's support for Hochul is a plus for the governor's bid for re-election. Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report

articles.title: Justice Department threatens legal action against California over alleged noncitizen voters
articles.summary: The Justice Department is threatening legal action against California unless state and local officials review a list of potential noncitizens on their voter rolls.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Justice Department is threatening legal action against California unless state and local officials review a list of potential noncitizens on their voter rolls. Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter sent letters to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan on Tuesday demanding that they review a list of possible noncitizens the federal government identified by noon on Thursday. “Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes,” McCotter wrote in letter, which was obtained by NBC News. “States are responsible for voter registration, and the Federal Government is responsible for maintaining immigration records to enable verification of citizenship. Working together, we can more effectively protect against voter dilution and promote election integrity.” McCotter wrote that they provided a password-protected thumb drive with a list of individuals the federal government “believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot” for the 2026 election. He asked that election officials “segregate — not cancel — those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots” until their citizenship status was determined. “The Department of Justice sent letters to California election officials demanding immediate action to ensure that noncitizens who automatically received ballots per California law do not vote in the upcoming federal election,” a Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement. “This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring.” Reuters first reported on the letters. Weber and Logan did not immediately respond to requests for comment. All registered voters in California receive mail-in ballots, which started going out on Oct. 5. The legal threats came amid a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what voting experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizens. Trump has long made unfounded claims that voting is marred by widespread fraud. Election officials in a several states — including Georgia, Connecticut, Nevada, and Washington state — say they have received federal subpoenas in recent months for election records. Some officials said they fear these actions were designed to set up possible legal challenges after the midterm elections. “What we have seen is some groundwork laid out for post-election challenges,” said Stuart Holmes, the director of elections in Washington State. “Whether that’s the seizure of voting equipment, ballots themselves, tabulation equipment ... we’re preparing for any and all eventualities in that case.” Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, a Democrats said officials in his state are also preparing for potential challenges to this November’s results. He added that he viewed the administration’s moves as “an effort to dissuade people from participating in the elections.” “You have a president who’s trying to choose the voter base rather than the voters choosing the elected, and that’s not how our democracy works,” he said in an interview. “It’s the people control our elections, and when you try to take that control out, you do it through intimidation, you do it through threats, and you do it by trying to dissuade people from participating.” Since Trump took office, his administration has brought over 100 cases involving allegations of voting by non-citizens. More than 154 million people voted in the 2024 election, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. During the second Trump administration, The Justice Department has sought voter registration data from every state in the country. It has filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., for refusing.
